title: Abu Bakr is back
body: Some time ago you sold Abu Bakr ten loads of linen. He remembers a good neighbour. A friend of his has a boat going to Alexandria, with room for your goods at no charge. He asks for a small favour in return.

choices.label: Take the place and do the favour
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars now and pays back 7 in two seasons. Abu Bakr is pleased.

choices.label: Take the place and skip the favour
choices.hint: It costs nothing now, and 7 dinars come in two seasons. Abu Bakr is not pleased.

note: Boats carried goods between Cairo, Alexandria and Qus on the Nile. In 1326 Ibn Battuta went down the river from Qus to Cairo in eight nights, in the flood.

sources.at: vol. 1, p. 69; the boat from Qus to Cairo in the flood

title: The silk has come
body: Some time ago you found silk for the rich family. It has come from Damascus, and the family is waiting. Nabil knows another buyer who may pay more.

choices.label: Sell to the family as agreed
choices.hint: Nabil is glad. The family may come back.

choices.label: Sell to the other buyer
choices.hint: More money. The family will hear of it.

note: Silk and linen were among the cloths that passed through Alexandria and Cairo.

sources.at: pp. 168 to 172; silk and linen in Alexandria and Cairo

title: Rahel offers first pick
body: Some time ago you split the difference with Rahel over the weight of her indigo. Now a new shipment of dyes has come. She offers you first pick before anyone else.

choices.label: Buy the best dyes at her price
choices.hint: It costs 5 now and pays 4 in two seasons. Dyers pay well.

choices.label: Wait for the price to fall
choices.hint: You keep your money and gain 3 in two seasons, and buyers abroad hear that you wait for a fair price.

note: Al-Maqrizi wrote that Cairo had 54 markets. Fustat had 19.

sources.at: Introduction n. 11; the count of markets in Cairo and Fustat

title: Farid's ship never came
body: Some time ago you lent Farid 5. His ship was lost at sea. He has paid back 4, which is all he has. He asks you to forgive the rest.

choices.label: Forgive the rest
choices.hint: You get 1 back in four seasons. Farid will not forget it.

choices.label: Ask for the rest over a year
choices.hint: You may get 2 in four seasons. Farid will be hurt, and the court likes a clear book.

note: Sailing in the Mediterranean in winter was risky, though ships did sail.

sources.at: p. 277 and p. 294; winter bans were a legal fiction, and winter voyages were made

title: The price of gold is falling
body: Some time ago you bought two chests of gold while the Malians were in Cairo. Now they have gone on to Mecca, and gold sells for less. Jamil says the price may fall again.

choices.label: Sell the gold now
choices.hint: Jamil pays 164 dinars for the two chests, 82 for each. Before the Malians came, a chest sold for 100. The gold leaves your warehouse, and your partners think well of you in two seasons.

choices.label: Hold on to the gold
choices.hint: Any gold in your warehouse stays there, worth whatever Cairo pays for it. Nothing comes to you now.

note: Al-Umari wrote that the price of gold fell after the king of Mali came to Cairo. Another scholar doubts that the fall lasted for years.

sources.at: pp. 269 to 273; al-Umari on the price of gold in Cairo
the long effect of the visit is disputed

title: The inspector found the sacks
body: The muhtasib's men found out where the bad dates went. You are fined, and your neighbours saw it. Bishr asks how you wish to answer.

choices.label: Say sorry in the market
choices.hint: It is hard to say. People will respect it.

choices.label: Say the sacks were not yours
choices.hint: It saves face for now, and 4 come in two seasons.

note: The muhtasib of 1341 punished the poultry seller in public, for all to see.

sources.at: section 1, n. 95; the punishment of 1341 in the public eye

title: Yehuda owes you a favour
body: Some time ago your carter took Yehuda's goods on his day of rest. Now a buyer at Alexandria wants glass, and Yehuda knows him. He offers to send the buyer to you.

choices.label: Take the buyer
choices.hint: It costs 4 now to fill the order and may pay 7 in two seasons. Alexandria hears of it.

choices.label: Pass the buyer to a friend
choices.hint: You gain good will, not money.

note: Jewish and Muslim merchants had long called each other business friends and done each other favours.

sources.at: p. 281, as quoted by Edwards and Ogilvie (2008), p. 17

title: Amina says thank you
body: Some time ago you bought three loads of sugar from Amina when she needed money. Now she offers you a place in her next pressing at a good price.

choices.label: Buy a place in her next pressing
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars now and may pay 11 later. Other merchants hear of it.

choices.label: Thank her with a gift
choices.hint: It costs 3 dinars now and 1 comes back in two seasons. She will remember it.

note: Four of the 13 refineries owned by merchants were managed by Karimi.

sources.at: p. 149; the managers of the merchants' refineries

title: Kamil's boat has arrived
body: Some time ago you sent four loads of sugar with Kamil. His boat reached Alexandria, and the buyers paid. He asks you to ship with him again next year.

choices.label: Agree to ship with him next year
choices.hint: In four seasons you get 4. He will keep a place for you.

choices.label: Keep your choice open
choices.hint: In four seasons you get 5. You can pick the best boat each year.

note: The Nile flooded in late summer, after the rains on the hills of Ethiopia. Ibn Battuta saw the flood in July 1326.

sources.at: p. 125 and the section on the flood; the monsoon rains on the Ethiopian highlands
vol. 1, p. 69; the flood season of 1326

title: Binyamin comes back
body: Some time ago you paid Idris and Binyamin each what he claimed. Now Binyamin says his cousin also put money in. He wants the same treatment.

choices.label: Pay the cousin too
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now and 3 come back in two seasons. Your name grows.

choices.label: Show him the ledger first
choices.hint: It may hurt his pride now. You keep 4 dinars, and a fair count is respected later.

note: Merchants did not rely on friendship alone. When a quarrel over money would not end, they took it to the courts.

sources.at: pp. 11 and 13 to 14; friendship beside formal partnerships, and the courts

title: Girgis remembers
body: Some time ago you looked after the son of Girgis's partner. Now Girgis offers you a share in his next trip to Damascus.

choices.label: Take a share of his trip
choices.hint: It costs 5 now and may pay 8 in three seasons.

choices.label: Ask for a letter of introduction
choices.hint: It costs nothing. It opens doors.

note: Some friendships between merchants lasted for a lifetime. A few went on for generations.

sources.at: pp. 169 to 170, as quoted by Edwards and Ogilvie (2008), p. 11

title: News from the funduq
body: Some time ago you took a share of the Karimi funduq. Now Khalid hears from merchants staying there that a road may close. He tells you first.

choices.label: Send a rider to warn your agents
choices.hint: It costs 8 dinars now and 2 more later. Your agents will be glad.

choices.label: Keep the news to yourself
choices.hint: It brings 3 dinars later, but it is not kind.

note: The Karimi were a loose group of merchants. They were not one company.

sources.at: p. 150; a loose confederation

title: Zubayda wants a standing deal
body: Some time ago you took Zubayda's offer to sell in her market. She asked a small fee. Now she wants you to sell with her every season.

choices.label: Agree to a standing deal
choices.hint: A fee of 3 dinars now, and 4 back in three seasons. It makes a steady friend.

choices.label: Sell where you like
choices.hint: You gain 3 dinars in two seasons, by choosing the best market. Zubayda will think you cold.

note: In Cairo, shops of one trade stood together. Al-Maqrizi's account says this saved time and the cost of carrying goods.

sources.at: Background n. 24; shops of one trade grouped for time saving and lower transport costs

title: Tamer has his title
body: Tamer was named chief of the merchants. He remembers who spoke for him. He offers you a share in his next shipment.

choices.label: Take a share in his shipment
choices.hint: It costs 5 now and may pay 8 in three seasons.

choices.label: Thank him and ask for nothing
choices.hint: It costs nothing. It shows you are not for sale.

note: One chief of the merchants held the title but was never regarded as an officer of the state.

sources.at: p. 152; Zaki al-Din al-Kharrubi and the title

title: Two bales were poor
body: Some time ago Salih bought six loads of linen for you. When the bales were opened, two were poor. Salih says the grower mixed them in. He offers to make it right.

choices.label: Ask him to pay for the two poor bales
choices.hint: You win back 20 dinars. Brokers talk now, and trust a house that checks later.

choices.label: Sell the two poor bales cheaply
choices.hint: You lose two loads of linen and gain 50 dinars.

choices.label: Call it a lesson
choices.hint: You gain no money, and you keep your linen. Salih buys better bales for you. In two seasons the brokers think well of your house.

note: A letter found in the Geniza told a merchant not to let a broker buy middling flax for the writer.

sources.at: pp. 278 to 279; the broker, the middling flax and the debased dinars

title: Yusuf wants it in writing
body: Yusuf has not forgotten the fee. He asks you to write down what the house owes him each time he goes out. He says words in writing last longer than words in the air.

choices.label: Write it down and seal it
choices.hint: It costs 2 dinars for a clerk. Yusuf feels easier.

choices.label: Say your word is good enough
choices.hint: You save the clerk's 2 dinars. Yusuf is more uneasy.

note: In the Geniza papers partners made up their accounts every year.

sources.at: p. 327; accounts made every year

title: Samir wants a share, not a wage
body: Samir has not forgotten the count. He says he will not go for a plain wage again. He asks for a third of the profit, so that he is paid by what he earns.

choices.label: Give him a third of the profit
choices.hint: He carries the risk of his own work.

choices.label: Keep him on a wage
choices.hint: You keep the whole profit, and the house gains 3 coins in two seasons. He may not stay.

choices.label: Let him go
choices.hint: He goes to another house, and pays back 3 coins he owes.

note: In the Geniza contracts the traveller's share was normally one third.

sources.at: p. 317; the worker's share, normally one third

title: Matteo wants to work again
body: Matteo took the house's fee. He asks to work for the house again. This time he wants the house's seal on his orders, so that other traders know who he works for.

choices.label: Give him the house's seal
choices.hint: It costs nothing now and 5 dinars in three seasons, if his debts fall on you. He carries your name.

choices.label: Pay him a fee for one more job
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now and brings 6 in two seasons. He stays free to go.

choices.label: Thank him and let him go
choices.hint: He leaves you a small gift.

note: In the Geniza papers a special job was paid with a fee of its own.

sources.at: p. 316; the commission paid for a special service

title: Raiders on the Aydhab road
body: A carter writes from Qus. Raiders of the desert, the Bedouin, have been troubling the caravans that go to Aydhab. A caravan is a group of travellers and animals that go together. Merchants are asking about safer ways.

choices.label: Hire an escort for your goods
choices.hint: It costs 8 dinars now. The escort keeps the goods safe, and partners hear of it.

choices.label: Send the goods by Quseir
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now and 3 more in two seasons. The sea road is longer but safer.

choices.label: Wait and see
choices.hint: It costs nothing. If the raiders come, your goods may be late.

note: One historian thinks that raiders troubled the caravans from Qus to Aydhab all through the early 1300s. So merchants and pilgrims began to seek safer routes.

sources.at: p. 458 (reporting Jean-Claude Garcin, 1976)

title: Costs on the far side
body: Isaac's accounts have come, and they show costs you did not expect. Goods sent over the sea pay for repacking, freight and customs. Some of the fees went to officials as small gifts. Isaac asks if you accept the accounts.

choices.label: Accept the accounts
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. There is no quarrel, and your partners trust you.

choices.label: Ask for every cost, one by one
choices.hint: It costs 1 dinar now, for the letters. Isaac is hurt, and he trusts you less.

choices.label: Offer to settle half
choices.hint: It costs 3 dinars now. Isaac takes it, and foreign houses think you fair.

note: In a lawsuit of 1097, a merchant listed the costs of sending goods over the sea. Repacking at Aydhab cost a quarter dinar, freight to Dahlak six and a quarter, and customs six.

sources.at: pp. 189 to 190 and note 25

title: The wreck on the coast
body: A pilot brings bad news. A ship carrying goods of yours was wrecked on the Malabar coast, away from Calicut. The ruler's men are taking the cargo, as the law there allows.

choices.label: Claim the goods through a friend in Calicut
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. A friend in Calicut argues your claim, and foreign houses hear that your house fights for its goods.

choices.label: Accept the loss
choices.hint: It costs 3 dinars now, the part of the cargo you cannot save. Nothing more.

choices.label: Give a gift to the ruler's men
choices.hint: It costs 9 dinars now. The ruler's men give back part of the cargo. In two seasons 1 lot of pepper reaches your warehouse, and the court hears of it.

note: In every Malabar land except Calicut, goods from a wrecked ship belonged to the king. At Calicut the owners kept them, and Ibn Battuta wrote that this is why the town grew rich.

sources.at: vol. 4, pp. 815 to 816

title: A chief stops the caravan
body: A chief of the Hoggar Berbers has stopped a caravan of yours on the road to Tuat. He will not let it pass until he gets cloth. It is the month of Ramadan, when many Muslims fast. The caravan master asks what to do.

choices.label: Give him the cloth
choices.hint: It costs 8 dinars now. The caravan goes on, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Argue until he lets it pass
choices.hint: It costs 2 dinars now, for food while you wait. The chief is not pleased.

choices.label: Go round by another road
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. The way is longer, but partners like a safe caravan.

note: In 1353, in Ramadan, a Berber chief stopped Ibn Battuta's caravan until it gave him cloth. Ibn Battuta wrote that in Ramadan these Berbers do not raid; this is later evidence, after the game's years.

title: A present for the sultan
body: A Venetian envoy leaves a present with you for the sultan's household. He asks if you will see that it arrives.

choices.label: Carry it yourself
choices.hint: It costs 3 dinars now, for the road. A court friend remembers it.

choices.label: Pass it to a broker
choices.hint: It costs 1 dinar now. The broker keeps a part, and the court hears of it.

choices.label: Refuse the errand
choices.hint: It costs nothing. The envoy finds someone else.

note: In 1345 Venice set aside 800 gold ducats as a present for the sultan. It set aside 200 more for gifts to his lords.

sources.at: p. 137 and note 117

title: The lower rate runs out
body: The lower rate for Florentines is running out. The king's officer will take the word of the Bardi company's man as proof of who is Florentine.

choices.label: Ask the Bardi company's man to vouch
choices.hint: It costs 2 dinars now. He owes you a favour in return.

choices.label: Ship under a Genoese partner
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now, a larger fee. Foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Pay the full rate
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now. The king's officer thanks you.

note: The lower rate was renewed in 1325 and 1326, and made lasting in 1327. After that, the Bardi company's man could vouch that a trader was Florentine.

sources.at: Pagnini 1766 printing, p. 71 (the renewals of 1325 to 1327)

title: The king of Armenia grants a favour
body: An Italian writes from Ayas. The king of Armenia has freed his company from customs, the taxes on goods. He offers to carry your goods too.

choices.label: Send goods through him
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now, a share for him. The sale is quick, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Ignore the offer
choices.hint: It costs nothing. He finds another partner.

choices.label: Hold your goods in his warehouse
choices.hint: It costs 3 dinars now. The goods are safe, and partners hear of it.

note: In 1335 the king of Lesser Armenia let Pegolotti's firm trade free of customs. Most other foreigners paid 4 in 100 each way.

sources.at: Pagnini 1766 printing, p. 45

title: A friendly letter
body: A new lord of Tabriz sends you a friendly letter. He promises peace and the return of stolen goods. He invites you to send a load.

choices.label: Send a load
choices.hint: It costs 12 dinars now. If the letter is true, foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Send a small test load
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now. It is a careful start, and partners like that.

choices.label: Refuse
choices.hint: It costs nothing. The lord is offended.

note: In 1344 a Genoese chronicler tells that the ruler of Tabriz wrote to Genoa promising peace and stolen goods back. Genoese merchants trusted him, and he took goods worth 200,000 pounds.

sources.at: vol. 2, p. 131 (reporting Stella)
